Number of Islands (DFS on a grid)
O(rows × cols)
Course Schedule: topological sort with Kahn's algorithm
O(V + E)
Dijkstra: shortest path in a weighted graph
O((V + E) log V). It doesn't work with negative edges; use Bellman-Ford for those.
Rotting Oranges (multi-source BFS)
Clone Graph (deep copy of an undirected graph)
The original-to-clone map doubles as the visited set. Putting the clone in the map before visiting neighbours prevents infinite recursion on cycles. O(V + E) time and space.
Detect a cycle in a directed graph with DFS (and return a topological order)

A plain visited array is not enough for directed graphs: you must distinguish "on the current path" from "already finished". Reverse postorder gives a topological order (Course Schedule II). O(V + E). For undirected graphs, a cycle is a visited neighbour that is not the parent, or use Union-Find.
Is Graph Bipartite? (two-colouring)

BFS from every uncoloured node (the graph may be disconnected), giving neighbours the opposite colour. A conflict means an odd cycle, so the graph is not bipartite. O(V + E). "Possible Bipartition" is the same problem with an edge list.
Pacific Atlantic Water Flow
Reverse the question: instead of flowing down from every cell, flood uphill from each ocean's border and intersect the two reachable sets. O(R·C) instead of O((R·C)²).
Surrounded Regions (capture 'O's not connected to the border)
Same "start from the border" trick: anything reachable from an edge 'O' survives, and every other 'O' is captured. O(R·C). On very large grids prefer BFS to avoid deep recursion.
Word Ladder (shortest transformation sequence)

Each word is a node; edges connect words one letter apart. BFS finds the shortest path in an unweighted graph. Generating 26·L neighbours per word avoids comparing all pairs. O(N · L² · 26) with string building. Bidirectional BFS is the usual follow-up optimisation.
Cheapest Flights Within K Stops (Bellman-Ford)

Bellman-Ford relaxes every edge V−1 times and handles negative weights; one more round that still improves a distance means a negative cycle. Limiting it to k+1 rounds and copying the array each round enforces the stop limit. O(k · E). Plain Dijkstra fails here because the cheapest path may use too many stops.
Minimum Spanning Tree: Prim's algorithm (Min Cost to Connect All Points)

Prim grows one tree, always adding the cheapest edge leaving it (like Dijkstra, but keyed on edge weight instead of total distance). O(E log V). Kruskal is the alternative: sort all edges and add each one whose endpoints are not yet connected, using Union-Find. It suits sparse edge lists; Prim suits dense graphs.
BFS vs DFS: when do you choose each?

| BFS | DFS
Structure | Queue | Recursion or stack
Shortest path (unweighted) | Yes | No
Memory | O(width of frontier) | O(depth); recursion can overflow on big grids
Natural for | Levels, minimum steps, multi-source spread (Rotting Oranges) | Connected components, cycle detection, topological order, all paths
Time | O(V + E) | O(V + E)
Rule of thumb: "minimum number of steps" → BFS. "Does a path exist / count components / explore everything" → either, and DFS is usually shorter to write.
Shortest paths: BFS vs 0-1 BFS vs Dijkstra vs Bellman-Ford

| BFS | 0-1 BFS | Dijkstra | Bellman-Ford
Edge weights | All equal | 0 or 1 | Non-negative | Any, negative allowed
Structure | Queue | Deque (0 to front, 1 to back) | Min-heap | Relax all edges V - 1 times
Time | O(V + E) | O(V + E) | O((V + E) log V) | O(V · E)
Detects negative cycles | N/A | N/A | No | Yes (a V-th round still relaxes)
Limit on number of edges | No | No | Not directly | Yes: k + 1 rounds = at most k stops
Rule of thumb: pick the simplest one the weights allow. Negative weights or "at most k edges" → Bellman-Ford; otherwise Dijkstra.
Adjacency list vs adjacency matrix vs edge list

| Adjacency list | Adjacency matrix | Edge list
Space | O(V + E) | O(V²) | O(E)
Is u-v an edge? | O(degree) | O(1) | O(E)
List neighbours of u | O(degree) | O(V) | O(E)
Best for | Sparse graphs, BFS / DFS | Dense graphs, Floyd-Warshall | Kruskal, Bellman-Ford
Rule of thumb: interview graphs are almost always sparse, so build an adjacency list from the edge list first.
Topological sort: Kahn's algorithm (BFS) vs DFS postorder

| Kahn (in-degree + queue) | DFS (three colours)
Order produced | Directly, as nodes reach in-degree 0 | Reverse of postorder
Cycle detection | Fewer than V nodes output | Meeting a node that is "in progress"
Recursion depth risk | None | O(V) stack depth
Extras | Easy to get the lexicographically smallest order with a min-heap; easy to count "levels" (semesters) | Fits naturally when you already have DFS code
Time | O(V + E) | O(V + E)
Interview tip: Kahn's is easier to get right under pressure and has no stack-depth risk; mention DFS as the alternative.
Minimum spanning tree: Prim vs Kruskal

| Prim | Kruskal
Grows | One tree from a start vertex | A forest, merging components
Main structure | Min-heap of edges leaving the tree | Edges sorted by weight + Union-Find
Time | O(E log V) with a heap; O(V²) with arrays | O(E log E) for the sort
Best for | Dense graphs (e.g. all pairs of points, use the O(V²) version) | Sparse graphs given as an edge list
Rule of thumb: edge list given → Kruskal. Complete graph of points (Min Cost to Connect All Points) → array-based Prim in O(V²), which avoids building V² edges.
